To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hospital volume has a strong effect on accuracy of hospital report card and that hospital volume has to be >100 before ≥70% hospitals are accurately classified.

the accuracy of hospital performance reports is, at best modest, when case volumes are low and that, for many cardiovascular conditions, case volumes must be very high (≥300) before hospital report cards are accurate.
provider volume has a strong effect on report card accuracy, and that the accuracy of report cards is modest when provider volumes are small to medium, but high when provider volumes are large.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accuracy of hospital performance indicators in settings in which case volumes are small and the accuracy of risk adjustment is imperfect.

the effect of case volume on the validity and utility of hospital report cards, and it provides a framework for the design and implementation of hospital report cards that are more accurate and more useful.
the accuracy of hospital comparison report cards.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the volume of a hospital’s case load has a significant influence on the accuracy of a hospital report card, but the accuracy of hospital performance reports is still modest, even for large hospital case volumes.
the accuracy of hospital comparison reports depends on the number of cases, the number of variables, and the quality of the risk-adjustment algorithm used to adjust for patient differences.
the accuracy of report cards is modest at best, even with perfect risk adjustment, and the accuracy of report card comparisons is dependent on the volume of the providers being compared.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hospital report cards are useful only when provider volume is large.
hospital report cards are useful for providers with high volume, and for providers with lower volume they should be used with caution.
hospital volume is a key factor that should be considered when interpreting hospital report cards.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when provider volumes are low, hospital report cards should be interpreted with extreme caution.
hospital volume has a strong effect on report card accuracy, and that this effect is independent of any other factors.
, when provider volumes are small, hospital report cards may have little value.
